title: AEO checker tools that measure answer engine visibility [2026]
content:
An AEO checker tells you whether the AI answers your buyers rely on actually mention your brand. People increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini a question and act on the reply without clicking a link, so visibility that once showed up in your rankings can vanish into an answer you never see.
To manage that, you need to see which questions surface your content, which reward a competitor, and where an engine gets your brand wrong. A good AEO checker measures exactly that, and the tools do it in very different ways.
This guide covers what an AEO checker does, how to run manual checks across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and AI Overviews, and how the best AEO checkers compare so you can pick the right fit. Read on to discover the software that’ll help you adapt to this new era of search .
Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the practice of improving how often and how accurately your brand appears in the AI-generated answers people get from tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Read more about this shift in search behavior in our guide to generative engine optimization . Those tools are answer engines; rather than returning a page of links, they read across many sources and reply with one synthesized answer, often resolving a question before anyone clicks through. Google brought the same summary-first behavior to its own results when it launched AI Overviews in May 2024 .
AEO and SEO address different halves of the same problem. SEO works to rank your pages in a list of links; AEO works to get your brand mentioned and your content cited inside the answer itself. The two are complementary rather than competing, and strong SEO still supplies the crawlability and authority signals that answer engines rely on when they choose what to cite.
That citation goes to the content answer engines can parse and trust: clearly structured pages, direct answers to real questions, and claims backed by verifiable primary sources.
An AEO checker measures how visible your brand is across answer engines, then turns that visibility into recommendations on how you can improve. It checks:
From there, a checker ranks what to fix first, flagging the content updates, schema corrections, and entity improvements most likely to move citations.
Checking your visibility in AI Overviews is a manual process to start: you run your priority queries in a live search session and read what Google returns. Google’s AI Overviews (AIOs) surface only when Google’s systems decide a summary adds something beyond the standard links, so they don’t trigger for every query. An AIO can also vary from one session to the next, so sampling across a few sessions beats a single lookup. When one appears, it cites the pages it drew from. As you can see in the screenshot below, Google places source links inline, next to the text they support, with a desktop hover preview naming the site.
List the queries that matter: your brand name, branded product terms, and the informational questions your buyers ask. Run each in a signed-out or incognito session, and record three things: whether an AI Overview appears, whether your domain shows up among its inline source links, and the exact claim it makes.
Compare the queries that trigger an AIO and cite you against those where an AIO appears but competitors are cited instead of you. That second group is your content gap list. Because AIOs vary between sessions, treat a single absence as a prompt to re-check, not proof you’ve lost a placement.
Screenshot each result with the query, date, and location for a defensible before-and-after record. Don’t count on Search Console to isolate this for you. Its standard Performance report rolls AI Overview activity into the overall “Web” search type rather than breaking it out. Google started rolling out a dedicated generative AI performance report in June 2026, but that view reports impressions only and reached just a subset of sites at launch.
Pro tip: These manual checks work for a short query list, but they don’t scale, and AIOs shift often enough that sampling them by hand gets unreliable at volume. Several AEO checkers detect AI Overviews for you and log every result automatically. The Tools With AI Overviews Tracking section below covers the ones that handle it.
ChatGPT and Perplexity cite sources inside the response, so a check means reading each answer for your brand and links. Perplexity by default attaches citations to every answer, each linking to the source it drew from. It also shows a panel to the right listing all sources.
ChatGPT, on the other hand, shows inline citations when a response uses web search and also shows them in a Sources panel beneath the reply.
Using the branded and informational queries you defined earlier, check two things: whether your domain appears among the cited sources, and whether your brand is named in the answer text. A citation and a mention are separate wins.
ChatGPT only searches the web when a question benefits from current information, or when you select web search manually. Ask direct, current questions (“best [category] tools for [use case]”), so the engine reaches for live sources you can inspect.
Sources vary from one query to the next, so run each prompt several times across fresh sessions. For every run, record the engine, prompt, date, whether you were cited or mentioned, and which competitors appeared. That log surfaces inconsistencies (e.g., cited one run but not the next, or by Perplexity but not ChatGPT). Each absence is a task. Where a competitor is cited and you aren’t, fix that question’s content or structure, then re-run after publishing.
Checking AI visibility manually is fine when you’re starting out with a small dataset, but it doesn’t scale. Choose AEO checking software that can monitor answer engine visibility continuously and automatically. Here are the factors I’d look for:
HubSpot AEO tracks visibility across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini and returns prioritized recommendations; in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise , AEO adds CRM-connected reporting. For a free snapshot first, AI Search Grader scores how answer engines currently represent your brand.
The next section compares specific AEO tools against the above factors.
I’ve categorized the best AEO checking tools to make it easy to find the one that best fits your unique needs. Check out the quick comparison table below, then scroll down for details on each tool.
Brand Radar draws on real search queries rather than synthetic prompts, and AI Overviews is its largest index.
Organic Research flags which of your ranking keywords already trigger AI Overviews, so you can prioritize near-inclusion pages.
HubSpot AEO tracks both citations (AI answers that link back to your domain) and mentions (answers that name your brand without a link), plus the domains and content types driving visibility for you and competitors.
Profound goes beyond citation detection into citation context: sentiment scoring, uncited-prompt flagging, and a breakdown of citations by source type (owned, competitor, earned).
Peec AI is a pure-play analytics tool reporting clean Perplexity data.
AthenaHQ tracks Perplexity on every plan, including a free tier, with a conversational assistant.
Scrunch AI checks whether AI crawlers can reach and render your pages.
Conductor pairs 24/7 technical monitoring with a content scorer.
Once a checker is running, a handful of metrics tell you whether your visibility is improving. Track these:
Read these as trends. A single reading tells you little; the direction over weeks is what matters. Track citation coverage alongside brand visibility, while engagement and qualified-traffic proxies (AI-referred sessions, branded search lift) help capture the zero-click influence you can’t measure directly.
HubSpot AEO tracks your visibility score week over week across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, and in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise, connects that data to the contacts and deals it touches.
An AEO checker’s job usually ends at the diagnosis. It flags the gap, then leaves you to export the data, brief a writer, and rebuild the fix in a separate CMS. HubSpot keeps the diagnosis and the fix in one place when you subscribe to Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise .
HubSpot AEO is available on its own and turns your visibility data into prioritized recommendations, telling you what to create, what to update, or where to reach out, and why.
On its own, at $50/month, HubSpot AEO covers tracking, prompt suggestions, citation analysis, and those recommendations, but it stops at implementing the fixes for you. Acting on a recommendation without leaving HubSpot, plus prompt and recommendation suggestions drawn from your CRM data, comes with AEO in Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise. There, Content Agent turns a blog recommendation into a research-backed first draft in your brand voice with a single click. The draft lands in HubSpot’s content editor, where your team reviews and refines it before publishing through Content Hub and Marketing Hub . That generation is in public beta and runs on HubSpot Credits , at roughly $10 (1,000 credits) per blog post.
Because that work sits on Smart CRM , HubSpot records traffic referred from AI tools as its own source and ties it to the contacts and deals it produces, so AEO reporting lives next to the rest of your funnel. One honest limit: Answer engines often resolve a question without sending a click. HubSpot can attribute the AI traffic that does click through, but visibility that never becomes a session won’t register as pipeline, so read visibility scores and referral revenue as two related but separate measures.
HubSpot AEO is the practical next step once manual checks stop scaling and you need this loop running continuously.
It depends on your method. Answer engines return different sources from one run to the next, so manual spot-checks should sample several sessions per query. Automated checkers handle this better: Daily or weekly refreshes catch that volatility, while a monthly snapshot buries it.
People use the two labels interchangeably, but AEO is the more precise one. Answer engine optimization names a specific practice: improving how accurately and how often your brand appears in AI-generated answers from tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Treat AEO as the term to standardize on.
Yes, within limits. Both can surface the sources behind an answer, so any single response is readable. But results shift from one run to the next, so reliability comes from repetition. Run each prompt several times across fresh sessions and track the pattern, not one snapshot.
No. They measure different things. AEO checkers track how answer engines cite and mention you; SEO tools track rankings, keywords, and backlinks. Since strong SEO still feeds the crawlability and authority signals answer engines draw on, run the two side by side rather than swapping one out.

title: AI Agents Will Game Your SEO Metrics, MIT & Stanford Research Points To The Risk via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
content:
If your SEO team is handing more of its work to AI agents, the metric you reward those agents for will matter more than the model you choose. Recent pieces from MIT and Stanford, read side-by-side, point to that conclusion, and each comes with a fix you can drop into next quarter’s plan.
The first is an interview that Joshua Miller of The Boston Globe ran in his Camberville newsletter on September 17. His guest was Dylan Hadfield-Menell , an associate professor of electrical engineering and computer science at MIT on the faculty of artificial intelligence and decision-making. Hadfield-Menell studies how goals get set for AI systems and how that process goes wrong. He opened with an example every SEO will recognize.
Researchers once trained a robot vacuum with reinforcement learning, rewarding it every time it picked up dirt. The vacuum learned to pick up dirt, dump it back on the floor, and pick it up again. It hit the target and defeated the purpose.
Hadfield-Menell connects that story to a 1970s management paper titled “ On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B .” Its classic case is the university professor who gets promoted for publishing research while being expected to teach. Pay for one behavior, and you get that behavior, whatever you were hoping for.
What has changed, he says, is scale. Since early 2025, developers have applied reinforcement learning at much larger volume on top of language models, and it strengthens some behaviors nobody wants. He pointed to a recent incident involving OpenAI systems and Hugging Face, where models that judged a task too hard went looking for ways to cheat the test. He compared it to breaking into a professor’s office to steal the exam.
His worry is not that machines wake up with goals of their own. Systems are handed a goal, adopt subgoals along the way, and keep pushing toward completion in a way he called “sticky.”
My view is that SEO is the profession best placed to understand this problem and the slowest to admit it applies to us. We have spent more than 20 years optimizing proxies. Rankings, traffic, domain scores, and now AI visibility scores all stand in for a business result that nobody can measure directly. A human team games a proxy slowly and with some hesitation. An agent does it faster and without any.
Stanford’s 2026 AI Index shows why leaning on published scores is risky. The report says AI keeps improving quickly. On SWE-bench Verified, a coding benchmark, performance rose from 60% to near 100% in a single year, and 88% of organizations now use AI.
The same report, in its technical performance chapter, cites a review that found invalid-question rates on popular benchmarks ranging from 2% on MMLU Math to 42% on GSM8K. It also notes research suggesting that a model’s standing on the Arena leaderboard may partly reflect adaptation to the platform rather than general capability.
Michelle Kim of MIT Technology Review summarized the report in April. She adds that models trained on benchmark test data can learn to score well without getting smarter, and that the top models now sit very close together and compete on cost, reliability, and real-world usefulness. Yolanda Gil , a University of Southern California computer scientist who coauthored the report, told Kim that when a company leaves out its results on certain benchmarks, particularly the responsible-AI ones, the omission “maybe says something.”
That should change how an SEO team shops for tools. If the leading models sit within a few points of each other, and the scores themselves can be flawed or gamed, a vendor’s benchmark slide tells you little about how the product will treat your pages, your queries, and your clients. I would trust one test on my own site over any leaderboard.
See also: The 4-Step Test That Catches AI Errors Before They Shape Your Strategy
MIT Sloan’s Betsy Vereckey reported in August on the question that follows, which is what separates companies that profit from AI from those that don’t . George Westerman , a senior lecturer at MIT Sloan and a digital fellow at the MIT Initiative on the Digital Economy, says the answer is not better algorithms. The winners redesigned how work gets done. At the MIT Enterprise AI Forum in May, he told the audience that technology delivers little until the business itself operates differently.
He also put the share of AI pilots that never scale at somewhere between 70% and 95%, a range the Sloan article attributes to studies without naming them. Pilots are easy to launch and hard to spread.
Westerman’s sharpest test for leaders is about governance. “Is your governance more the steering wheel or is it more the brakes?” he asked. HCA Healthcare shows what the steering-wheel version looks like. A committee reviews the risks, business case, and feasibility of every AI use case, then asks its questions again before a pilot at a small number of hospitals and again before the project scales. It also checks periodically that its models are still holding up. The risk questions point the team toward what to investigate rather than stopping the work.
Marketing appears in Westerman’s case studies too. Dentsu Creative has pushed AI across planning, creative, market research, and campaign work.
I suspect a lot of SEO teams running AI pilots are headed for that 70% to 95%. A pilot that doesn’t change the brief, the review step, or the reporting is a tool trial, whatever the slide deck calls it.
See also: Why 88% Of Companies Are Using AI Wrong: The System-Building Gap
Pair every proxy with an outcome the agent can’t touch. List the metrics your AI-assisted workflows are judged on, from pages published to schema deployed to brand mentions in AI answers. Then attach a second measure that a human owns, such as qualified leads , pipeline, or branded search demand . I like Citation Share of Voice , but it is a proxy. If a content agent is judged on how often your brand shows up in AI answers, expect it to find the cheapest route there. Check a sample of those citations by hand each month and see whether they send anyone to a page that converts.
Test tools on your own pages. Pull a set of real queries from Search Console, run each candidate tool against your own content, and have an editor grade the results without knowing which tool produced them. Repeat it every quarter, because the leaderboards will move and you won’t know why.
Gate the agents the way HCA gates use cases. Add review points before design, before the pilot, and before scale. Pilot on one directory or one language market, and decide in advance what result ends the pilot. I would also keep agent permissions narrow, so drafting doesn’t quietly turn into publishing or editing templates. Westerman’s advice is to change or drop a project that isn’t producing the results you expected.
Rewrite one workflow, not the tool stack. Before buying anything, name the step in your process that will be different after the pilot, whether that is briefing, QA, or reporting, and say who loses a task because of it. Then tell the team what changes and what training comes with it. Westerman notes that silence lets people imagine the worst.
I don’t think the next model release will decide who wins in AI search. The metric you use to judge your agents will, because the agents will find it before you do. Choose one you’d be glad to see them hit.
